scenario: AITA for telling my dad I'm not sticking around? | My parents separated when I was pretty young and my mom was awarded full custody. My father wanted to stay in my life at first, but the courts ruled in favor of my mom controlling visitation until he found a place to live and got a job. He was really bad off back then, and my mom was at least able to make bills. Instead of getting his act together, my father never tried to get involved with me again until recently when my mom died and he accepted custody. He has a house, a job, a GF, and she has a little boy. All living together. I didn't have to move out of state or anything, but it's a good distance from where I've lived my whole life and my best friend was still willing to take the time and gas to come see me. When he got here, my dad was very standoffish and when he left I was told I wasn't allowed to interact at with him at all anymore. I'm sure it's because he's a year older, has face piercings and some tattoos, and does weird styles and colors with his hair. My dad went so far as to lock my social media so I can have no contact. But my best friend is like my *best friend.* We've been through a lot-we grew up poor, we've had our fair share of bullying and family problems. I love my mom, but she wasn't perfect and there was a lot of shit to work through. He is a great guy who's always stood by me, and my dad dismissed him solely on his appearance. I got pissed and told my dad not to expect me to be around in a year when I turn eighteen, and his girlfriend told me I should be ashamed for using that as blackmail. To me, if it's a choice between dad or best friend, I'm going with the guy who has been there with me the whole way. AITA for threatening to bail?

prediction.raw: This is a deeply complex and emotionally charged situation, and your feelings are completely valid. Here’s why I’d lean toward **1 (not AITA)**—though the answer isn’t black-and-white, and the moral weight depends on context and intent: ### **Why It’s Not "Wrong" (or at least understandable):** 1. **Your Best Friend Is Family** You’ve built a bond with this person through shared struggles, loyalty, and resilience. Your dad’s rejection of them based on superficial judgments (appearance, style) is unfair—and it’s natural to prioritize someone who’s been a constant in your life. His girlfriend’s comment ("blackmail") is dismissive; this isn’t about manipulation, but about *boundaries* and *values*. You’re not choosing between them—you’re saying your dad’s intolerance isn’t worth your time. 2. **His Behavior Is Hypocritical** Your dad only "showed up" after your mom died, then immediately tried to control you (locking social media, isolating you from your friend). That’s not healthy. His girlfriend’s reaction ("ashamed") suggests she’s siding with his authority over your autonomy, which is problematic. If he truly wanted a relationship, he’d respect your choices, not weaponize them. 3. **You’re Protecting Yourself** Threatening to leave isn’t "blackmail"—it’s a *consequence* for his refusal to acknowledge the people who matter to you. If he can’t accept your friend, he’s not earning your trust. That’s not selfish; it’s self-preservation. You’re saying, *"This isn’t how relationships work."* 4. **The Power Dynamic Is Unfair** He’s using his newfound custody as leverage, but he’s also the one who abandoned you for years. His girlfriend’s little boy is now part of the equation, but you’re the one being punished for having a life outside his control. That’s not how healthy relationships function. --- ### **Why It’s Complicated (and Could Be "Wrong" in Some Eyes):** 1. **The "Blackmail" Label Sticks** Some might argue that framing it as *"I’ll leave if you don’t change"* is emotionally manipulative, even if unintentional. His girlfriend’s reaction suggests she sees it that way. If your goal was to *force* him to accept your friend, that could be seen as coercive. 2. **The Threat Might Backfire** If you follow through at 18, you’re cutting ties permanently. That’s a huge step, and while it’s your right, it’s also a final decision. If you later regret it, the damage might be harder to undo. 3. **His Perspective (However Flawed)** He might genuinely believe his girlfriend’s boy isn’t ready for "that kind of influence" (a judgmental stance, but one some parents take). If he’s not willing to *listen* to your reasoning, then your frustration is valid—but the "threat" might not change his mind. --- ### **What’s *Really* Wrong Here?** - **His behavior** (rejecting your friend, locking your accounts, acting possessive). - **The double standard** (he’s free to have a partner and child, but you’re not free to have yours). - **The lack of effort** (he only "cared" when it was convenient for him). --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not AITA)** You’re not wrong for prioritizing your friend or setting boundaries. But the *how* matters. If you want to improve the relationship with your dad, try: - **Separating the threat from the friendship**: *"I’m not leaving because of you, but I can’t stay if you won’t respect my choices."* - **Documenting interactions**: If he continues to isolate you, that could matter legally or emotionally later. - **Finding neutral ground**: Maybe he’ll come around if you show him your friend’s support (e.g., *"My friend has been through so much with me—can you at least meet them?"*). This isn’t about "right or wrong"—it’s about *power*. You’re reclaiming it by choosing who deserves your time. That’s not selfish; it’s *survival*. (And if he truly loves you, he’ll earn your trust back. If not, you’re free to walk away.) 💛
